title: Offerings
hook: a birthday, eleven dollars, and a poet who gives away forests and lakes he doesn't own
tomorrow: when Shantideva gets scared, where does he run?

segments.voice: Chapter one ended on wishing and going: the wish is the map, the going is the road. Wish, then go. Chapter two opens with empty pockets.

A birthday is coming for someone you love, and your bank app says eleven dollars. You scroll gift guides anyway. Everything worth giving seems to cost more than you have, and the cheap stuff feels like an apology. So you start to wonder whether you should just send a card and say nothing. Shantideva stood exactly there, with nothing in his hands, wanting to give the best he could imagine. What he did next is the strangest gift list ever written.
screen: `ELEVEN DOLLARS.` → `THE CHEAP STUFF FEELS LIKE AN APOLOGY.` → `HE HAD NOTHING IN HIS HANDS.`

segments.voice: Chapter two opens with offerings to the Buddhas, the teaching and the bodhisattvas. And then a confession in the middle of it: I have no merit, I'm poor, I have nothing else to give. So he offers what nobody owns. Flowers and fruit. Healing herbs. Clear, cool water. Mountains, and quiet forests where trees bend with blossoms. Lakes covered in lotuses, with the cry of wild geese. Crops growing in the fields. All of it, as far as space goes, belonging to no one. Here's the move that makes it work. Offering, in Buddhist practice, isn't a payment. A flower on an altar doesn't buy anything. It's a way of turning toward what you love and saying: this, for you. So a lake you'll never own can still be given, because the giving is in the turning. And then he goes one step further, and offers himself: his whole body and life, to the Buddhas and their children, to use as they will. The person with eleven dollars has more than they think. The light on the street at six o'clock. A walk to the place they love. Your full attention for an afternoon. Offer the unowned.
screen: `I HAVE NOTHING ELSE TO GIVE.` · `FORESTS, LAKES, WILD GEESE.` · `AN OFFERING IS NOT A PAYMENT.` · `THEN HE OFFERS HIMSELF.` · then, large: `OFFER THE UNOWNED.`

segments.voice: Look out the nearest window, or at the sky, or at one plant in the room. Choose one beautiful thing in sight that belongs to no one. Rest your eyes on it for the whole sit, and in your own words, silently, give it to someone you love.
Offerings: what Shantideva gives when his hands are empty. Forests, lakes and fields that no one owns, and finally himself.
Your line: offer the unowned. The sky was never for sale, and it can still be a gift. Chapter two, begun.

howItsDone: Buddhists often set out flowers, water, light and incense at a shrine as offerings, and some Tibetan practices offer the whole world in the imagination, as Shantideva does in this chapter.

what a scholar hears: the chapter's offerings become a model for later Mahayana practice, where the whole world is offered in the imagination, and the gift of oneself comes last.

chat.says: ông's birthday is sunday. i have $11. everything good costs more. what do i even give him?
options: Something nobody owns: drive him to see the maples at sunset, and draw them with him.
Wait till you've saved more. A cheap gift says you didn't really try.
Skip the gift. He'd rather you save money than spend it on him.
chat.meaning: With empty hands, Shantideva offers forests and lakes no one owns. An offering is a turning toward someone, not a price tag.
